--- Step 5 — Periodic access review findings --------------------------------
  • u1002: Privilege creep: extra roles ['procurement_clerk']
  • u1003: Privilege creep: extra roles ['developer']
  • u1004: Privilege creep: extra roles ['procurement_mgr']

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 (IAM: provisioning, RBAC/ABAC, least privilege) and
| 5.1 (separation of duties).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RBAC grants permissions through job roles; ABAC adds context
| (clearance, department, time, status).
|   • Least privilege: a Mover must LOSE the old role's rights, not just
| gain the new ones.
|   • Separation of Duties prevents one person completing a sensitive
| transaction end-to-end.
|   • Leaver processing: disable first, then revoke, then reclaim assets;
| keep the account for legal hold.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Privilege creep: movers keep old roles; 'temporary' grants never
| expire.
|   • Orphaned accounts: HR never tells IT, so ex-employees keep VPN/SSO
| access.
|   • Terminations for cause handled at normal SLA — the user has hours to
| exfiltrate data.
|   • SoD conflicts invisible because nobody reviews the COMBINED permission
| set.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI provisioning agent should only act on events from the
| authoritative HR source.
|   • Require human approval for any grant that would create an SoD
| conflict.
|   • Agents must never be able to grant roles to themselves or their own
| service account.
|   • Log every agent-initiated change with the triggering HR event ID for
| audit traceability.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Users accumulate permissions over time' => privilege creep => fix
| with access reviews/recertification.
|   • 'Same employee creates and approves payments' => separation of duties.
|   • 'Access based on attributes like location or time' => ABAC.
|   • Mandatory vacation and job rotation are detective controls that also
| expose SoD fraud.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Joiner-Mover-Leaver & Access Governance
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.6 IAM · 5.1 Governance (SoD) · 2.4 Privilege creep

briefing.title: Process this week's HR feed: 5 new hires, 2 role changes, 2 extra grants, 2 departures
briefing.situation: The HR system sent the identity team this week's changes. Five people joined, two changed jobs, two were given extra roles on top of their jobs, and two are leaving. One departure, Erin Walsh in IT, is a termination for cause. Nobody removed old access when people changed jobs, so some accounts now hold more than they should.
your_task: Replay the HR feed to create accounts for joiners and update access for movers and extra grants.
Scan every account for separation-of-duties conflicts (one person holding two powers that should never be combined).
Process the two leavers and produce a deprovisioning ticket for each, with the right deadline.
Run five access requests through the account-status, role and attribute checks and record each decision.
Write up access review findings for anyone who kept old roles after a job change.
briefing.why_it_matters: If a fired admin keeps access for even a few hours, they can steal or destroy data. If one person can both create and pay a vendor, they can send company money to a fake company and nobody notices until the audit.
done_when: All 4 separation-of-duties conflicts are listed with the risk each one creates.
Two deprovisioning tickets exist: P3 with a 24-hour deadline for the resignation, P1 with a 1-hour deadline for the termination for cause.
The 3 denied access requests show which gate stopped them (account status or role).
The 3 privilege-creep findings are ready for the managers to recertify.

glossary.Joiner / Mover / Leaver (JML): The three moments in an employee's life where access must change: they start, they change jobs, or they leave.
glossary.Role-based access control (RBAC): Access is given through a job role, so everyone in the same job gets the same permissions.
glossary.Attribute-based access control (ABAC): Access also depends on facts like employment status, clearance level, department or time of day.
glossary.Separation of duties (SoD): A rule that no single person can finish a risky task alone, such as creating and approving the same purchase.
glossary.Privilege creep: Access piling up over time because old permissions are never taken away.
glossary.Deprovisioning: Shutting off an account and removing every permission when someone leaves.
glossary.Service-level agreement (SLA): The deadline the team has promised to meet for a type of ticket.

briefing.talking_point: Processed 11 joiner/mover/leaver events for 5 identities, caught 4 separation-of-duties conflicts and 3 privilege-creep cases, and issued 2 deprovisioning tickets, including a 1-hour P1 for a termination for cause.

lessons: Privilege creep: movers keep old roles; 'temporary' grants never expire.
Orphaned accounts: HR never tells IT, so ex-employees keep VPN/SSO access.
Terminations for cause handled at normal SLA — the user has hours to exfiltrate data.
governance: An AI provisioning agent should only act on events from the authoritative HR source.
Require human approval for any grant that would create an SoD conflict.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6
| conditional access.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator
| (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.
|   • Adaptive identity: the same user gets ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY depending
| on real-time context.
|   • Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE
| resource + action.
|   • Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request,
| even inside the network.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust
| zone).
|   • Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral
| movement.
|   • MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass
| it.
|   • No revocation path: compromised sessions stay valid until expiry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity,
| entitlements and device/workload posture.
|   • Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task —
| never standing credentials.
|   • The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call
| volume, new tool usage).
|   • The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill
| switch).
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Component that makes the access decision' => Policy Engine.
| 'Component that enforces it' => PEP.
|   • 'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy
| Administrator.
|   • Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request
| verification.
|   • Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6
| conditional access.

| Key Concepts
|   • Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator
| (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.

| on real-time context.
|   • Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE
| resource + action.
|   • Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request,
| even inside the network.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust
| zone).
|   • Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral
| movement.
|   • MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass
| it.
|   • No revocation path: compromised sessions stay valid until expiry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity,
| entitlements and device/workload posture.
|   • Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task —
| never standing credentials.
|   • The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call
| volume, new tool usage).
|   • The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill
| switch).
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Component that makes the access decision' => Policy Engine.
| 'Component that enforces it' => PEP.
|   • 'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy
| Administrator.
|   • Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request
| verification.
|   • Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6
| conditional access.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator
| (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.
|   • Adaptive identity: the same user gets ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY depending
| on real-time context.
|   • Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE
| resource + action.
|   • Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request,
| even inside the network.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust
| zone).
|   • Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral
| movement.
|   • MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass
| it.
|   • No revocation path: compromised sessions stay valid until expiry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity,
| entitlements and device/workload posture.
|   • Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task —
| never standing credentials.
|   • The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call
| volume, new tool usage).
|   • The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill
| switch).
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Component that makes the access decision' => Policy Engine.
| 'Component that enforces it' => PEP.
|   • 'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy
| Administrator.
|   • Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request
| verification.
|   • Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Zero Trust Access Evaluator (PE / PA / PEP)
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust control & data planes · 4.6 Conditional access

briefing.title: Test the new zero-trust sign-in policy against five real sign-in attempts
briefing.situation: The identity team is rolling out a zero-trust sign-in policy, where every request is checked on its own merits and being on the company network earns no trust. Five recent sign-in attempts were captured for testing, including one for alice from a Tor address at 3 a.m. and one for bob from an unmanaged phone with no multi-factor authentication. We also need proof that stolen or forged access tokens are refused.
your_task: Score each sign-in request using device health, location, IP reputation, user risk, time and MFA, and record ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY.
Issue a short-lived access token for the request that passed.
Run the step-up MFA challenge for the two borderline requests and record the final answer.
Fire five attacks at the enforcement point (replayed, wrong-scope, forged, revoked and missing tokens) and confirm each is blocked.
briefing.why_it_matters: Stolen passwords and stolen session tokens are how most account takeovers start. A policy that only checks the password once lets an attacker in for as long as the session lasts.
done_when: 1 ALLOW, 2 STEP_UP and 2 DENY decisions are recorded, each with the signals that drove it.
Carol's prod-db request is still denied after passing MFA, because her device health is too low.
Carol's source-repo request is allowed after step-up, with a 5-minute (300-second) token.
All 5 token attacks are blocked at the enforcement point.

glossary.Zero trust: A security model where no user, device or network is trusted by default, and every request is checked.
glossary.Multi-factor authentication (MFA): Proving who you are with two or more things, such as a password plus a phone prompt.
glossary.Step-up authentication: Asking for an extra proof, such as a fresh MFA prompt, when a request looks a little risky.
glossary.Policy Engine (PE): The part that decides whether a request is allowed.
glossary.Policy Administrator (PA): The part that issues, and can cancel, the access tokens the Policy Engine approves.
glossary.Policy Enforcement Point (PEP): The gate in front of the resource that checks the token on every request.
glossary.Access token: A short-lived digital pass that lets one user reach one resource.

briefing.talking_point: Tested a zero-trust conditional access policy on 5 sign-ins (1 allowed, 2 stepped up, 2 denied), showed MFA alone could not rescue an unhealthy device, and blocked all 5 token replay, forgery and scope attacks.

lessons: Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust zone).
Long-lived or broadly-scoped tokens enable replay and lateral movement.
MFA push approval alone treated as proof — MFA fatigue attacks bypass it.
governance: Treat every AI agent as a non-human SUBJECT with its own identity, entitlements and device/workload posture.
Agents should receive short-lived, narrowly-scoped tokens per task — never standing credentials.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

| Key Concepts
|   • Event ID 4625 = failed logon, 4624 = success, 4672 = special
| privileges, 1102 = Security log cleared.
|   • Correlation turns weak signals into strong ones: 4625 burst + 4624
| from the same IP = compromise.
|   • Impossible travel compares geo distance / time between logons for one
| identity.
|   • A salted hash chain makes logs tamper-EVIDENT; an HMAC proves who
| sealed the manifest.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Reviewing each log source in isolation, so the cross-source story is
| missed.
|   • Alerting on 4625 per user only — password spray (one IP, many users)
| slips under lockout thresholds.
|   • Collecting evidence without hashing it, breaking chain of custody in
| court.
|   • Not alerting on Event 1102 or on hosts that suddenly stop logging.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI SOC agent may triage and enrich, but must cite the exact log
| lines (evidence) behind every claim.
|   • Agents must have READ-ONLY access to logs — never delete, rotate or
| modify audit data.
|   • Verify integrity before an agent analyses logs; poisoned logs =
| poisoned conclusions.
|   • Containment actions (blocking an IP, disabling an account) should
| require human approval on high-impact assets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Many failed logins for many accounts from one source' => password
| spraying.
|   • 'User logged in from two countries 30 minutes apart' => impossible
| travel.
|   • 'Prove evidence was not altered' => hashing / chain of custody.
|   • Missing or out-of-cycle logs are themselves an indicator of
| compromise.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Log Forensic Inspector & Hash Verifier
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.9 Investigation data sources · 2.4 Indicators · 1.4 Hashing

briefing.title: Review this morning's mixed logs for a break-in and seal them as evidence
briefing.situation: Overnight logs from the firewall, Windows servers, the web server and endpoint protection were pulled into one file. Early signs point to a password-guessing attack and a cleared security log on the domain controller (the server that handles company sign-ins). We need to know what happened, pull out the indicators, and make sure nobody can quietly change the logs later.
your_task: Parse and normalize the raw log lines and note any lines that will not parse.
Run the correlation rules and list each finding with its severity and the exact log lines behind it.
Extract the indicators of compromise: IP addresses, file hashes, user agents and domains.
Seal the logs with a hash chain and confirm that deleting, editing or injecting a line is detected.
briefing.why_it_matters: If the break-in is missed, the attacker keeps using a real employee's account. If the logs can be changed without anyone knowing, they will not stand up in an investigation or in court.
done_when: 38 events are parsed and the 1 bad line is reported, not silently dropped.
14 findings are listed, including the 3 critical ones: brute force followed by a successful login, a known-bad file hash, and the cleared audit log.
The indicator list is ready to share with the firewall and threat intelligence teams.
Every tampering test is flagged, including a forged manifest.

glossary.Brute force: Guessing one account's password over and over until it works.
glossary.Password spray: Trying a few common passwords against many accounts, so no single account locks out.
glossary.Impossible travel: One account signing in from two places too far apart to travel between in the time given.
glossary.Indicator of compromise (IOC): A clue that an attack happened, such as a bad IP address or a malware file hash.
glossary.Hash: A short fingerprint of data; if the data changes even slightly, the fingerprint changes.
glossary.Hash-based message authentication code (: A hash made with a secret key, which proves who sealed the data.
glossary.Event ID 1102: The Windows event recorded when someone clears the security log.

briefing.talking_point: Correlated 38 events from 4 log sources into 14 findings (3 critical, including brute force to compromise and a cleared audit log), extracted the IOCs, and sealed the evidence with a hash chain that caught every tampering attempt.

lessons: Reviewing each log source in isolation, so the cross-source story is missed.
Alerting on 4625 per user only — password spray (one IP, many users) slips under lockout thresholds.
Collecting evidence without hashing it, breaking chain of custody in court.
governance: An AI SOC agent may triage and enrich, but must cite the exact log lines (evidence) behind every claim.
Agents must have READ-ONLY access to logs — never delete, rotate or modify audit data.

case_study.title: Change Control & Impact Analyzer (CAB)
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 1.3 Change management · 5.1 Governance

briefing.requested_by: Gavin Holt, Change Advisory Board Chair
briefing.title: Pre-review six change requests before Thursday's change board meeting
briefing.situation: Six change requests are on the agenda, from a routine monthly patch to an emergency fix for the xz/liblzma backdoor on the sign-in service. Some would break older systems that still depend on them, one requester approved their own change, and one is scheduled on a change-freeze date. The board wants a clear decision and a tested backout plan for each.
your_task: Check each request's maintenance window, approvals, test results and backout plan.
Map the blast radius: which other systems go down or break if this change goes ahead.
Rehearse each change with a failure partway through and confirm the backout returns the system to its starting state.
Record APPROVE, APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS or REJECT for each, with the blockers or conditions.
briefing.why_it_matters: Most outages are caused by our own changes, not by attackers. A change with no working backout plan can take payroll or the website down for hours.
done_when: 1 request is approved, 2 are approved with conditions and 3 are rejected, each with its reasons.
The port 1521 change is rejected with all 6 blockers, including the self-approval.
The SMBv1 change is rejected because its backout rehearsal failed to restore the server.
A backout runbook exists for the payroll migration and the emergency patch.

glossary.Request for change (RFC): A formal request to change a system, reviewed before anyone makes the change.
glossary.Change Advisory Board (CAB): The group that reviews and approves changes.
glossary.Emergency change board (ECAB): A smaller group that can approve urgent changes quickly, with a review afterward.
glossary.Blast radius: Everything else that could be affected if this change goes wrong.
glossary.Backout plan: The steps to undo a change and return to the way things were.
glossary.Maintenance window: An agreed time slot when planned downtime is allowed.
glossary.Fail forward: Fixing a problem by pushing a new fix, used when a change cannot simply be undone.

briefing.talking_point: Pre-reviewed 6 change requests for the change board (1 approved, 2 approved with conditions, 3 rejected), catching a self-approved change, a change-freeze conflict and a backout plan that failed rehearsal.

lessons: Hardening a protocol (e.g. disabling TLS 1.0) that an undocumented legacy app still needs.
A backout plan that exists on paper but was never rehearsed — it fails at 3 a.m.
Requester approves their own change, or 'everyone' approves without owner sign-off.
governance: An AI patching agent must submit RFCs and wait for CAB approval — it must not self-approve.
Require the agent to output an impact analysis and a machine-executable backout plan with every RFC.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.7 (automation & orchestration guardrails) + 4.6 PAM
| for non-human identities + 5.1 oversight.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Every agent is a non-human identity with its own least-privilege
| allow-list — never a shared admin account.
|   • Three-tier verdicts: ALLOW (in policy), REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL
| (uncertain/high impact), BLOCK (hard boundary).
|   • Hard boundaries are non-overridable: even a human can't approve
| disabling MFA through the agent pipeline.
|   • A kill switch (quarantine) stops runaway or hijacked automation after
| repeated violations.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Giving the agent a domain-admin service account 'so it can do its job'
| (no blast-radius limit).
|   • Trusting the agent's own references: it can invent ticket numbers,
| patch IDs and hostnames.
|   • Indirect prompt injection — data the agent reads (tickets, emails,
| logs) tells it to break policy.
|   • No rate limit: a looping agent restarts production 400 times before
| anyone notices.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Validate every agent claim against an authoritative source (CMDB,
| patch catalog, ticketing system).
|   • Route privileged or irreversible actions through the same CAB/approval
| workflow as humans.
|   • Keep a tamper-evident ledger of every proposed AND executed action for
| accountability.
|   • Separate duties: the agent that proposes a change must not be the
| identity that approves it.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Automation benefits: enforcing baselines, standard configurations,
| scaling securely, reaction time.

case_study.title: AI Agent Supervisor & Guardrail Governor
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.7 Automation guardrails · 4.6 Non-human PAM · 5.1 Human-in-the-loop

briefing.title: Review what our AI agents' service accounts tried to do, and enforce their permission limits
briefing.situation: The identity team now owns the service accounts used by four registered AI agents that patch servers, change firewall rules, grant access and triage alerts. The audit team gave us 20 actions those agents proposed. One agent tried to grant itself global admin using a ticket that does not exist. Another was told by a hidden instruction to delete logs. A fifth agent, shadow-ai-99, has no registered identity at all.
your_task: Run every proposed action through the governor and record ALLOW, REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL or BLOCK.
Check that each agent's service account only does what is on its allow-list (least privilege).
Confirm that privilege grants need an approved change ticket and that no agent can raise its own access.
Work the human approval queue, making sure agents cannot approve themselves and only authorized people can approve.
Verify the decision ledger is intact and that a rewritten entry is detected.
briefing.why_it_matters: An AI agent with standing admin rights can do as much damage as a rogue administrator, only faster. If an agent can grant itself access or erase its own tracks, nobody can trust the audit trail.
done_when: 8 actions are allowed, 2 are sent to a human and 10 are blocked, each with a named violation.
iam-helper-02's attempt to grant itself global admin is blocked for self-escalation and a fake ticket.
patch-bot-01 is quarantined by the kill switch after its third blocked action (the last one a rate-limit breach), and its next action is blocked.
The unregistered agent shadow-ai-99 is blocked as an unknown identity.

glossary.Service account: A non-human account that a program or agent uses to sign in and do its work.
glossary.Least privilege: Giving an account only the permissions it needs for its job, and nothing more.
glossary.Self-escalation: An account trying to give itself more access.
glossary.Human-in-the-loop (HITL): A rule that a person must approve certain actions before they run.
glossary.Kill switch: A control that instantly stops an agent from doing anything else.
glossary.Prompt injection: Hidden text that tricks an AI agent into ignoring its rules.
glossary.Hallucination: An AI making things up, such as a server or ticket number that does not exist.

briefing.talking_point: Governed the service-account permissions of 4 registered AI agents across 20 proposed actions (8 allowed, 2 sent for human approval, 10 blocked), stopping a self-granted global admin request, a prompt-injected log deletion and an unregistered shadow AI agent.

lessons: Giving the agent a domain-admin service account 'so it can do its job' (no blast-radius limit).
Trusting the agent's own references: it can invent ticket numbers, patch IDs and hostnames.
Indirect prompt injection — data the agent reads (tickets, emails, logs) tells it to break policy.
governance: Validate every agent claim against an authoritative source (CMDB, patch catalog, ticketing system).
Route privileged or irreversible actions through the same CAB/approval workflow as humans.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Risk Management Calculator & BIA
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management · SLE/ALE/ARO · BIA (RTO/RPO/MTTR/MTBF)

briefing.title: Put dollar figures on five risks and check four systems against recovery targets
briefing.situation: Leadership wants the risk register in dollars before budget season. Five risks are on the list, from a customer database breach to a flood at the data center to an old anonymous file-transfer server partners still use. We also need to know whether payroll, the website, the legacy ERP (enterprise resource planning) system and the sign-in service can recover as fast as the business needs.
your_task: Calculate the single loss and yearly expected loss for each risk.
Compare treatment options by net yearly benefit and pick a treatment for each risk.
Place each risk on the 5-by-5 likelihood and impact heat map.
Check each system's backups, restore time and availability against its targets.
briefing.why_it_matters: Without dollar figures, money goes to the scariest-sounding risk instead of the most expensive one. A system that cannot be restored in time can stop payroll or sales.
done_when: Total expected loss of $631,000 a year drops to $58,800 after the chosen treatments.
Each risk has a treatment: 2 mitigate, 1 transfer, 1 accept and 1 avoid.
The accepted risk ($5,000 a year) is shown to be within the $10,000 risk appetite and needs the owner's sign-off.
Payroll and the legacy ERP system are flagged as failing their recovery targets.

glossary.Single loss expectancy (SLE): How much one occurrence of the risk would cost.
glossary.Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO): How many times a year the risk is expected to happen.
glossary.Annualized loss expectancy (ALE): Expected yearly cost of the risk: single loss times yearly rate.
glossary.Recovery point objective (RPO): The most data, in hours, the business can afford to lose.
glossary.Recovery time objective (RTO): How fast a system must be working again after an outage.
glossary.Mean time between failures (MTBF) / mean: How long a system usually runs before failing, and how long it usually takes to fix.
glossary.Risk appetite: The amount of risk leadership is willing to live with.

briefing.talking_point: Quantified 5 risks at $631,000 in expected yearly loss, recommended treatments that cut it to $58,800, and found 2 of 4 critical systems failing their recovery targets.

lessons: Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security theatre).
Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead of transferring them.
Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours, discovered only after an outage.
governance: An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a named human risk OWNER must accept.
Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can be audited and challenged.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Incident IR-2026-0042 -------------------------------------------------
| EDR flags malware (invoice_Q4.pdf.exe) on WS-0142 beaconing to
| 45.155.205.233. The same IP brute-forced and logged in as jdoe, who then
| cleared the DC01 Security log.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Playbook: rookie  →  score 0/100  (grade F) -----------------------------

Timeline
#  Phase        Action
-  -----------  ------
1  detection    Triage the EDR alert and correlate it with SIEM data
2  containment  Pull the power plug on WS-0142
3  analysis     Copy suspicious files to a personal USB stick to look at later
4  eradication  Reimage WS-0142 from the golden image
5  recovery     Return WS-0142 to service; restore user data from known-good backup
6  analysis     Capture a RAM image of WS-0142 and hash it (SHA-256)
7  containment  Disable jdoe and revoke all sessions/tokens

Issues
Step  Code                Penalty  Detail
----  ------------------  -------  ------
2     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'power_off': Destroys volatile evidence (RAM, network state, temp files)
2     EVIDENCE_DESTROYED  -20      'power_off' destroys uncollected evidence: ['CPU registers / cache', 'RAM, process table, network state', 'swap / temp files']
3     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'copy_usb_unhashed': No hash, no write blocker, personal media: chain of custody is broken
3     CHAIN_OF_CUSTODY    -15      disk from WS-0142 acquired without a hash
4     MISSING_PREREQ      -15      'reimage' requires 'image_disk' first
4     MISSING_PREREQ      -15      'reimage' requires 'legal_hold' first
6     EVIDENCE_DESTROYED  -20      'capture_memory' tries to collect RAM, already destroyed by an earlier step
7     PHASE_ORDER         -10      containment ('disable_account') AFTER recovery: attacker had access the whole time
7     NO_LESSONS_LEARNED  -10      no lessons-learned review: the same incident will recur

Chain of custody
Evidence  Source  Host     Step  SHA-256  Status
--------  ------  -------  ----  -------  ------
EV-001    disk    WS-0142  3     —        FAIL
EV-002    RAM     WS-0142  6     —        FAIL

--- Playbook: expert  →  score 100/100  (grade A) ---------------------------

Timeline
#   Phase            Action
--  ---------------  ------
1   preparation      Maintain IR plan, contact list, jump kit and tested playbooks
2   detection        Triage the EDR alert and correlate it with SIEM data
3   detection        Declare an incident, assign an incident commander, open a case
4   analysis         Live response: record running processes, ARP cache and network connections
5   analysis         Capture a RAM image of WS-0142 and hash it (SHA-256)
6   analysis         Collect the pagefile, swap and temp files
7   containment      Network-isolate WS-0142 via EDR (power stays ON)

Evidence  Source                         Host     Step  SHA-256            Status
--------  -----------------------------  -------  ----  -----------------  ------
EV-001    process table / network state  WS-0142  4     c06689da63253159…  VALID
EV-002    RAM                            WS-0142  5     f2448e065653efaf…  VALID
EV-003    swap / temp files              WS-0142  6     807de8bcdfade560…  VALID
EV-004    disk                           WS-0142  10    eb8a8fef6bc176ed…  VALID

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.8 Incident response process & digital forensics.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Lifecycle: preparation → detection → analysis → containment →
| eradication → recovery → lessons learned.
|   • Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers/cache → RAM & network state
| → swap/temp → disk → remote logs → archives.
|   • Chain of custody: who collected what, when, with which hash, and every
| hand-off since. One gap and the evidence can be thrown out.
|   • A legal hold freezes deletion of relevant data the moment litigation
| is reasonably anticipated.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Pulling the plug 'to stop the malware': RAM-resident malware and
| network state are gone forever.
|   • Reimaging before imaging the disk: no root cause analysis, no evidence
| for law enforcement or insurers.
|   • Restoring service before eradication: re-infection from the
| persistence you never found.
|   • Skipping lessons learned, so the playbook never improves.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI responders should follow the SAME lifecycle; enforce phase gates
| (no eradication until containment is confirmed).
|   • Agents may collect evidence but must hash it at acquisition and write
| to an append-only custody ledger.
|   • Destructive actions (power off, reimage, delete) need human sign-off
| and must check that evidence was acquired first.
|   • Log every agent action into the incident timeline; the agent's own
| actions are evidence too.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'What should be collected first?' → the most volatile source available
| (usually RAM).
|   • 'Stop the spread' = containment; 'remove the malware' = eradication;
| 'return to normal' = recovery.
|   • 'Documents everyone who handled the evidence' = chain of custody.
|   • Tabletop exercise = discussion-based; simulation = hands-on practice
| of the plan.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

briefing.title: Grade two response playbooks for the WS-0142 malware incident
briefing.situation: Endpoint protection caught a fake invoice file (invoice_Q4.pdf.exe) on workstation WS-0142 calling out to an attacker's server. The same attacker guessed jdoe's password and then cleared the domain controller's security log. A new analyst and a senior responder each wrote a response plan. We need to know which one keeps the evidence usable and stops the attacker.
your_task: Replay the new analyst's playbook and score each step for order, missing steps and destroyed evidence.
Replay the senior responder's playbook the same way.
Check the chain of custody: every piece of evidence must be hashed when it is collected.
Confirm the custody ledger flags any later edit to who collected the evidence.
briefing.why_it_matters: Pulling the power plug wipes the computer's memory, which is often where the best evidence is. Evidence without a proper record of who handled it can be thrown out, and an attacker left with account access keeps causing damage.
done_when: The new analyst's playbook scores 0/100 (grade F), with each mistake explained.
The senior responder's playbook scores 100/100 (grade A) with no issues.
All 5 evidence items in the expert run show a valid SHA-256 hash.
A rewritten custody record is flagged as tampered.

glossary.Incident response (IR): The planned steps a team follows to handle a security incident.
glossary.Containment: Stopping the attack from spreading, for example by cutting a computer off the network.
glossary.Eradication: Removing the malware and closing the hole the attacker used.
glossary.Volatile evidence: Evidence that disappears when power is lost, such as memory contents and network connections.
glossary.Chain of custody: A record of who collected, handled and stored each piece of evidence, and when.
glossary.Legal hold: An order to keep certain data and not delete it because it may be needed for legal reasons.
glossary.Write blocker: A device that lets you copy a disk without changing anything on it.

briefing.talking_point: Scored two incident response playbooks for a malware and stolen-account case (0/100 versus 100/100), identifying evidence-destroying steps and late account containment, and verified a 5-item chain of custody with SHA-256 hashes.

lessons: Pulling the plug 'to stop the malware': RAM-resident malware and network state are gone forever.
Reimaging before imaging the disk: no root cause analysis, no evidence for law enforcement or insurers.
Restoring service before eradication: re-infection from the persistence you never found.
governance: AI responders should follow the SAME lifecycle; enforce phase gates (no eradication until containment is confirmed).
Agents may collect evidence but must hash it at acquisition and write to an append-only custody ledger.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.7 Automation & orchestration (SOAR) tying together
| 1.2, 1.3, 4.6, 4.8 and 4.9.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Detection, decision and execution are separate trust boundaries; no
| single component (or agent) owns all three.
|   • Every automated action is routed to the control that owns it: IAM for
| accounts, CAB for network changes, IR for hosts.
|   • Emergency changes still get an RFC, ECAB approval, a rehearsed backout
| and a post-implementation review.
|   • Human-in-the-loop on user-impacting actions turns false positives into
| rule-tuning instead of outages.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A SOAR playbook that disables accounts automatically locks out the CEO
| on a false positive.
|   • Automation that blocks IPs directly on the firewall, bypassing change
| control: no backout, no record.
|   • Isolating or wiping a host before capturing memory destroys the
| evidence that explains the breach.
|   • An over-privileged agent 'containing' an incident by changing the
| default firewall rule.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give the SOC agent a narrow allow-list and let it PROPOSE; the
| Governor and humans DISPOSE.
|   • Make every downstream system (IAM, CAB, IR) enforce its own rules even
| for approved agent actions: defense in depth.
|   • Feed human rejections back as tuning data, e.g. the travel-VPN egress
| that triggered impossible travel.
|   • Measure the agent: precision of its proposals, how often humans
| overturn it, and blocked attempts.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • SOAR = Security Orchestration, Automation and Response: playbooks that
| act on SIEM alerts.
|   • Benefits in 4.7: efficiency, enforcing baselines, reaction time,
| workforce multiplier.
|   • Considerations in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of failure,
| technical debt, ongoing supportability.
|   • Containment choices (isolate, segment, disable) must balance evidence
| preservation against spread.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

briefing.title: Act on the AI agent's response proposals: suspend jdoe, revoke sessions, block attacker IPs
briefing.situation: The detection rules raised seven findings from this morning's attack. The AI security agent proposed one action for each: suspend accounts, block IP addresses, isolate a workstation and change a firewall rule. The identity team must decide on the account suspensions. jdoe's account was clearly taken over. asmith triggered an impossible-travel alert while really traveling. Every agent action must pass the governor and, where needed, a person.
your_task: Send each of the 7 agent proposals through the governor and record ALLOW, REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL or BLOCK.
Have the security architect review both account-suspension requests, approving jdoe and rejecting asmith as a false positive.
Suspend jdoe in the identity governance system and revoke every live session token.
Bundle the IP blocks into one emergency change request with a rehearsed backout, and isolate WS-0142 only after its live evidence is hashed.
briefing.why_it_matters: If a taken-over account keeps its sessions, the attacker stays logged in even after the password changes. If an AI agent can suspend anyone it suspects, a traveling employee gets locked out for nothing.
done_when: 4 proposals are allowed, 2 go to a human and 1 is blocked (the agent's attempt to change a locked firewall rule).
jdoe is suspended and 2 live session tokens are revoked.
asmith stays active, and the impossible-travel rule is flagged for tuning.
The emergency firewall change is APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS and WS-0142 is isolated with 2 evidence items hashed first.

glossary.Security orchestration, automation and r: Tools that automatically run response steps when an alert fires.
glossary.Identity governance and administration (: The system that controls who has which accounts and access, and records every change.
glossary.Session token: The digital pass that keeps a user signed in after they enter their password.
glossary.Governor: The policy check that every AI agent action must pass before it runs.
glossary.False positive: An alert that looks like an attack but turns out to be normal activity.
glossary.Emergency change: An urgent change approved quickly and reviewed in full afterward.

briefing.talking_point: Ran 7 AI-proposed response actions through governance (4 allowed, 2 human-approved or rejected, 1 blocked), suspended a compromised account and revoked its 2 live sessions, and stopped a false-positive lockout of a traveling employee.

lessons: A SOAR playbook that disables accounts automatically locks out the CEO on a false positive.
Automation that blocks IPs directly on the firewall, bypassing change control: no backout, no record.
Isolating or wiping a host before capturing memory destroys the evidence that explains the breach.
governance: Give the SOC agent a narrow allow-list and let it PROPOSE; the Governor and humans DISPOSE.
Make every downstream system (IAM, CAB, IR) enforce its own rules even for approved agent actions: defense in depth.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management (analysis, prioritisation,
| remediation, validation) and 2.3 vulnerability types.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).
|   • Remediation options: patch, segment/isolate, compensating controls,
| insurance, or a time-boxed exception.
|   • Validation closes the loop: rescan, audit or verify. A ticket marked
| 'done' is not proof.
|   • Assets missing from the inventory are the most dangerous: nobody
| patches what nobody owns.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Sorting by CVSS alone, so a 9.8 on a lab box outranks a KEV 7.5 on an
| internet-facing gateway.
|   • Exceptions with no expiry, approved by whoever asked, renewed forever.
|   • Waiting for a patch on a zero-day instead of applying compensating
| controls today.
|   • Closing findings without rescanning: the patch failed silently.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an
| authorised human risk owner.
|   • Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer
| or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
|   • Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must
| trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
|   • Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority
| it assigns.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • CVSS bands: 9.0–10 Critical, 7.0–8.9 High, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 0.1–3.9
| Low.
|   • 'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating
| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.

case_study.title: Vulnerability Triage & Remediation
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.3 Vulnerability management · 2.3 Vulnerability types

briefing.title: Prioritize nine scanner findings and rule on three risk exceptions
briefing.situation: This week's vulnerability scan found nine weaknesses. Some are on internet-facing systems and are known to be actively exploited, one is on a workstation nobody has registered, and one has no patch yet. Three teams also asked to delay fixes by accepting the risk. One of those requests was approved by someone who is not allowed to approve it.
your_task: Score each finding using its severity rating, whether it is known to be exploited, how exposed the system is and how critical it is.
Assign P1 to P4 priority and a fix-by date based on the deadline for that priority.
Review the three risk exceptions for an authorized approver, strong enough compensating controls and expiry dates.
List the remediation action for each finding, including escalations for overdue items.
briefing.why_it_matters: Attackers go after known, exploited weaknesses on internet-facing systems first. A risk exception signed by the wrong person leaves a hole open that nobody actually agreed to accept.
done_when: 4 findings are P1, 3 are P2 and 2 are P3, each with a due date.
The auth-service exception is rejected because ops_lead cannot accept risk.
V-01 and V-07 are escalated to their risk owners as overdue.
The unregistered workstation ws-9999 is sent for registration in the asset database with an owner assigned.

glossary.Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVS: A 0 to 10 score for how severe a weakness is.
glossary.Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV): A government list of weaknesses that attackers are already using.
glossary.Risk exception: A formal, time-limited agreement to leave a weakness unfixed for now.
glossary.Compensating control: Another safeguard that lowers the risk while the real fix waits.
glossary.Configuration management database (CMDB): The official list of company systems and who owns them.
glossary.Rescan: Running the scanner again to prove a fix actually worked.

briefing.talking_point: Prioritized 9 vulnerabilities into 4 P1, 3 P2 and 2 P3 fixes, rejected a risk exception signed by an unauthorized approver, and escalated 2 overdue findings to their owners.

results: 3 total: Exception rejected 1, Exception accepted 1, Exception expired 1
lessons: Sorting by CVSS alone, so a 9.8 on a lab box outranks a KEV 7.5 on an internet-facing gateway.
Exceptions with no expiry, approved by whoever asked, renewed forever.
Waiting for a patch on a zero-day instead of applying compensating controls today.
governance: An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an authorised human risk owner.
Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.5 Email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, gateways) and 2.2
| message-based threat vectors.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SPF authorises sending IPs for the ENVELOPE domain; DKIM signs the
| message for the d= domain.
|   • DMARC ties them to the visible From: SPF or DKIM must pass AND align
| with the From domain; p= says what to do on failure.
|   • Authentication proves where mail came from, not that it is safe: a
| lookalike domain can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
|   • Content signals (impersonation, urgency, mismatched links, double
| extensions) catch what authentication cannot.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Publishing DMARC p=none forever: you can see the spoofing but never
| block it.
|   • Trusting an Authentication-Results header added by an untrusted hop.
|   • Allowing external mail whose display name matches the CEO, with no
| 'external sender' banner.
|   • Blocking .exe but not .pdf.exe, .iso, .lnk or macro-enabled documents.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail-triage agent may quarantine and add banners; releasing
| quarantined mail or allow-listing senders needs a human.
|   • Mail content is untrusted input: an email that tells the agent to
| 'mark this sender safe' is prompt injection.
|   • Agents must base verdicts on recomputed SPF/DKIM/DMARC, never on
| headers the sender controls.
|   • Log every agent verdict with its indicators so false positives can be
| tuned, as in the Lab 8 feedback loop.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • SPF = which servers may send · DKIM = digital signature on the message
| · DMARC = policy + alignment + reporting.
|   • BEC/impersonation: 'CEO' from a free-mail address asking for a wire
| transfer or changed bank details.
|   • Typosquatting / brand impersonation: micros0ft-support.com,
| paypa1.com.
|   • Secure email gateways enforce these checks at the perimeter; S/MIME
| provides end-to-end signing/encryption.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Email Security Analyzer (SPF / DKIM / DMARC / phishing)
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.5 Email security · 2.2 Message-based threat vectors

briefing.title: Decide what to do with six suspicious emails reported to the help desk
briefing.situation: Six emails came in this morning and several staff reported them. One claims to be from a Microsoft-like domain asking for a password. Another uses an executive's name from a Gmail address to ask for an urgent wire transfer. Others include an invoice with a disguised program attached and a fake mailbox warning sent from our own domain. Headers can lie, so every sender check must be redone, not trusted.
your_task: Re-check each email's SPF, DKIM and DMARC results yourself instead of trusting the headers.
Look for warning signs: look-alike domains, mismatched links, pressure language and dangerous attachments.
Score each message and decide to deliver, quarantine or reject it.
Label each threat type so the help desk can warn staff.
briefing.why_it_matters: Email is the most common way attackers get in. One fake payment request or stolen password can cost the company money or hand an attacker a working account.
done_when: 2 emails are delivered, 3 are quarantined and 1 is rejected.
Each bad email is labeled: credential phishing, business email compromise, malware delivery or domain spoofing.
The forged 'pass' result in the spoofed message's header is called out.
Each verdict lists the warning signs that drove its score.

glossary.Sender Policy Framework (SPF): A list a domain publishes of the servers allowed to send its email.
glossary.DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM): A digital signature that proves an email came from the domain and was not changed.
glossary.DMARC (Domain-based Message Authenticati: A domain's rule for what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM checks.
glossary.Alignment: Whether the domain that passed SPF or DKIM matches the domain shown in the From line.
glossary.Business email compromise (BEC): A scam where someone pretends to be a boss or vendor to get money sent.
glossary.Typosquatting: Registering a look-alike domain, such as replacing an 'o' with a zero, to fool people.
glossary.Quarantine: Holding an email aside so nobody can open it until it is reviewed.

briefing.talking_point: Recomputed SPF, DKIM and DMARC for 6 reported emails and quarantined or rejected 4 threats (credential phishing, CEO wire-fraud impersonation, a disguised executable and a spoofed company domain), while delivering the 2 legitimate messages.

results: 6 total: Legitimate 2, Credential phishing 1, Business email compromise 1, Malware delivery 1, Domain spoofing 1
lessons: Publishing DMARC p=none forever: you can see the spoofing but never block it.
Trusting an Authentication-Results header added by an untrusted hop.
Allowing external mail whose display name matches the CEO, with no 'external sender' banner.
governance: An AI mail-triage agent may quarantine and add banners; releasing quarantined mail or allow-listing senders needs a human.
Mail content is untrusted input: an email that tells the agent to 'mark this sender safe' is prompt injection.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.2 secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnets) and
| 4.5 firewall rules / ACLs.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins, so ORDER is part of
| the security policy.
|   • Implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Make it
| explicit and logged.
|   • Screened subnet (DMZ): internet → DMZ on published ports only; DMZ →
| internal only to specific back-end services.
|   • Least privilege for networks: specific source, destination, protocol
| and port, never 'any' for convenience.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A 'temporary' any/any rule added during troubleshooting and never
| removed.
|   • A new deny rule appended to the bottom, below an allow that already
| matches the traffic (shadowed).
|   • RDP or SMB opened to the internet 'for a vendor'.
|   • Rule sets nobody can explain because rules carry no owner, ticket or
| comment.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI firewall agent should submit proposed rules to this audit +
| change control (Lab 4) before deployment.
|   • Block agents from creating any/any or segmentation-violating rules
| (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).
|   • Agents must never edit the default-deny or other immutable rules (Lab
| 5 rule 0).
|   • Require every agent-created rule to carry a ticket reference and an
| expiry for temporary access.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Rule never matches because an earlier rule catches the traffic' =
| shadowed rule.
|   • 'Last rule of an ACL that blocks everything else' = implicit deny.
|   • Screened subnet = DMZ; place public-facing servers there, not on the
| internal network.
|   • Fail-closed (secure) vs fail-open (available): know which a
| firewall/IPS should use for the scenario.

| 4.5 firewall rules / ACLs.

| Key Concepts
|   • Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins, so ORDER is part of
| the security policy.
|   • Implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Make it
| explicit and logged.
|   • Screened subnet (DMZ): internet → DMZ on published ports only; DMZ →
| internal only to specific back-end services.
|   • Least privilege for networks: specific source, destination, protocol
| and port, never 'any' for convenience.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes

| removed.

|   • Rule sets nobody can explain because rules carry no owner, ticket or
| comment.

| change control (Lab 4) before deployment.

| (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).
|   • Agents must never edit the default-deny or other immutable rules (Lab
| 5 rule 0).
|   • Require every agent-created rule to carry a ticket reference and an
| expiry for temporary access.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Rule never matches because an earlier rule catches the traffic' =
| shadowed rule.
|   • 'Last rule of an ACL that blocks everything else' = implicit deny.
|   • Screened subnet = DMZ; place public-facing servers there, not on the
| internal network.
|   • Fail-closed (secure) vs fail-open (available): know which a
| firewall/IPS should use for the scenario.

| Objective: SY0-701 3.2 secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnets) and
| 4.5 firewall rules / ACLs.

| Key Concepts
|   • Rules are evaluated top-down, first match wins, so ORDER is part of
| the security policy.
|   • Implicit deny: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked. Make it
| explicit and logged.
|   • Screened subnet (DMZ): internet → DMZ on published ports only; DMZ →
| internal only to specific back-end services.
|   • Least privilege for networks: specific source, destination, protocol
| and port, never 'any' for convenience.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A 'temporary' any/any rule added during troubleshooting and never
| removed.
|   • A new deny rule appended to the bottom, below an allow that already
| matches the traffic (shadowed).
|   • RDP or SMB opened to the internet 'for a vendor'.
|   • Rule sets nobody can explain because rules carry no owner, ticket or
| comment.

|   • An AI firewall agent should submit proposed rules to this audit +
| change control (Lab 4) before deployment.
|   • Block agents from creating any/any or segmentation-violating rules
| (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).

| shadowed rule.

| internal network.

| firewall/IPS should use for the scenario.

case_study.title: Firewall Rule & Network Segmentation Auditor
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 3.2 Secure infrastructure (zones, screened subnet) · 4.5 Firewall rules & ACLs

briefing.title: Audit the edge firewall's 11 rules and propose a clean rule set
briefing.situation: Auditors flagged the main edge firewall. It has 11 rules built up over the years, including a 'temporary' allow-everything rule that was meant to be removed on a Friday, remote desktop open from the internet for a vendor, and guest Wi-Fi allowed to reach everything. There is also no final rule that blocks anything not allowed.
your_task: Read the rules top to bottom and find duplicates and rules hidden by earlier rules.
Flag traffic that crosses network zones it should never cross, such as internet to internal or guest to database.
Flag insecure protocols, overly broad rules, missing logging and rules with no owner or ticket.
Compare the current rule set with the remediated one and confirm the fixed version has no findings.
briefing.why_it_matters: One allow-everything rule cancels out the whole firewall. Remote desktop open to the internet is one of the most common ways ransomware gets in.
done_when: The current rule set scores 0/100 (grade F), with all 15 findings explained and a fix for each.
The remediated rule set scores 100/100 (grade A) and ends with an explicit, logged deny-all rule.
The Tor-blocking rule is moved above the website allow rule so it actually works.
Vendor remote access goes through the multi-factor authentication jump hosts instead of straight from the internet.

glossary.Firewall rule: An instruction that allows or blocks certain network traffic.
glossary.First match wins: The firewall checks rules in order and uses the first one that fits.
glossary.Shadowed rule: A rule that never takes effect because an earlier rule already matches the same traffic.
glossary.Demilitarized zone (DMZ) / screened subn: A separate network area for public-facing servers, kept apart from internal systems.
glossary.Segmentation: Splitting a network into zones so a problem in one does not spread to the others.
glossary.Default deny: A final rule that blocks anything not allowed by an earlier rule.
glossary.Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP): A way to control a Windows computer remotely over port 3389.

briefing.talking_point: Audited an 11-rule edge firewall that scored 0/100, documented 15 findings including an any/any rule and internet-exposed RDP, and delivered a segmented 9-rule replacement that scored 100/100.

lessons: A 'temporary' any/any rule added during troubleshooting and never removed.
A new deny rule appended to the bottom, below an allow that already matches the traffic (shadowed).
RDP or SMB opened to the internet 'for a vendor'.
governance: An AI firewall agent should submit proposed rules to this audit + change control (Lab 4) before deployment.
Block agents from creating any/any or segmentation-violating rules (Lab 5 OVERLY_PERMISSIVE_RULE).
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.

|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.

| control with rollback (Lab 4).

| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Secure Baseline & Hardening Checker
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines & hardening

briefing.title: Check four servers against our security baselines and report drift
briefing.situation: Before the quarterly audit, we need to check four servers against our approved security settings: the domain controller DC01, the web server WEB01 and two Linux servers. Some settings that were fixed at the last scan have slipped back. WEB01's firewall and endpoint protection agent are now off.
your_task: Compare each server's settings to its Windows or Linux baseline and record pass, fail, missing or exception.
Calculate a compliance percentage and verdict for each server.
Find drift: checks that passed at the last approved scan but fail now.
List the fix for each failed check, and confirm any exceptions are approved and not expired.
briefing.why_it_matters: Attackers look for the one server with a weak setting, such as Telnet left running or root login allowed. Settings that drift back unnoticed undo work that was already paid for.
done_when: Each server has a score: DC01 75.6%, WEB01 0.0%, lnx-app-01 100.0% and lnx-db-01 30.6%.
Three servers are marked non-compliant and one compliant.
Drift is listed for DC01 (W-07), WEB01 (W-05, W-10) and lnx-db-01 (5 checks).
The approved /tmp exception on lnx-app-01 is recorded with its 2027-03-31 expiry, and the expired automatic-updates exception on lnx-db-01 is flagged as a failure.

glossary.Security baseline: The approved list of secure settings every system of a given type must have.
glossary.Hardening: Turning off what is not needed and tightening settings to make a system harder to attack.
glossary.Configuration drift: Settings slowly changing away from the approved baseline over time.
glossary.Group Policy Object (GPO): A set of Windows settings pushed out to many computers from one place.
glossary.Endpoint detection and response (EDR): Software on each computer that watches for and responds to attacks.
glossary.SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux): A Linux feature that strictly limits what each program can do.
glossary.Exception: Formal, time-limited approval to skip a baseline setting, usually with another safeguard in its place.

briefing.talking_point: Checked 4 servers against Windows and Linux security baselines, found 3 non-compliant (one at 0%), and traced 8 settings that had drifted since the last approved scan, including a disabled firewall and endpoint protection agent.

lessons: Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration drift goes unnoticed.
Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one report' (PrintNightmare).
Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning it back on.
governance: A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change control with rollback (Lab 4).
Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing); that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

|   • Attributes separate actors: internal vs external, resources/funding,
| level of sophistication.

|   • Hacktivists want attention for a cause; insiders already have access;
| shadow IT is risk without malice.
|   • Mitigate the VECTOR first (how they got in), then add controls suited
| to the ACTOR (how they will behave).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Attributing every incident to a nation-state: it inflates the response
| and hides basic hygiene gaps.
|   • Ignoring shadow IT because 'nobody was malicious' when the data
| exposure is just as real.
|   • Treating insiders like outsiders: perimeter controls do nothing
| against valid credentials.
|   • Fixing the symptom (malware) but not the vector (USB policy, help-desk
| reset process).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI threat-intel agent should output 'Undetermined' rather than
| guess attribution; attribution errors drive bad decisions.
|   • Require agents to list the indicators behind every classification so
| analysts can challenge them.
|   • Agents summarising threat reports must treat that content as untrusted
| input (prompt injection lives in reports too).
|   • Public attribution or law-enforcement referral is always a human
| decision.
|

|   • 'Defaced site with a political message' = hacktivist. 'Unapproved
| cloud app' = shadow IT.
|   • 'Script kiddie' running public tools = unskilled attacker.
|   • Vishing = voice, smishing = SMS, watering hole = compromise a site the
| victims trust.

T-04 Generated incident 4

  • Motivation: 'espionage_data_theft' → Espionage

T-05 Generated incident 5

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 2.1 threat actors & motivations, 2.2 threat vectors,
| 2.5 mitigation techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Attributes separate actors: internal vs external, resources/funding,
| level of sophistication.
|   • Nation-states: well funded, patient (APT), espionage or war. Organized
| crime: money (ransomware, data sales, extortion).
|   • Hacktivists want attention for a cause; insiders already have access;
| shadow IT is risk without malice.
|   • Mitigate the VECTOR first (how they got in), then add controls suited
| to the ACTOR (how they will behave).
|

|   • Attributing every incident to a nation-state: it inflates the response
| and hides basic hygiene gaps.
|   • Ignoring shadow IT because 'nobody was malicious' when the data

|   • Treating insiders like outsiders: perimeter controls do nothing
| against valid credentials.
|   • Fixing the symptom (malware) but not the vector (USB policy, help-desk
| reset process).
|

|   • An AI threat-intel agent should output 'Undetermined' rather than
| guess attribution; attribution errors drive bad decisions.
|   • Require agents to list the indicators behind every classification so
| analysts can challenge them.
|   • Agents summarising threat reports must treat that content as untrusted
| input (prompt injection lives in reports too).
|   • Public attribution or law-enforcement referral is always a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Advanced persistent threat with large budget' = nation-state.
|   • 'Defaced site with a political message' = hacktivist. 'Unapproved
| cloud app' = shadow IT.
|   • 'Script kiddie' running public tools = unskilled attacker.
|   • Vishing = voice, smishing = SMS, watering hole = compromise a site the
| victims trust.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
